Introduction
This White Paper discusses the design basis and development of Texas A&M’s Electric
Boat for the Promoting Electric Propulsion 2025-2026 Competition. Although the hull is the
same as the 2024-2025 competition boat, the electrical and propulsions systems have been
upgraded to achieve higher consistency. Many of the risks associated with the previous year’s
design have been mitigated by an upgraded hatch design for the lid. Additionally, research was
conducted into propeller design to combat the limited availability of RC boat props greater than
3 inches in diameter.

Background Research
Surface Drive
The driving system used in the design of the boat consists of several components that
were investigated, ordered, and assembled by hand. These components include stingers, drive
dogs, prop nuts, and flex collets. Utilizing these components in a simple design attached to the
aft end of the boat allows for the drive shaft to be positioned at an angle to completely submerge
the propellers. This allows for easier maneuverability, improved thrusting at lower speeds, and
better efficiency for acceleration.
Propeller Efficiency
Propeller efficiency is important to any boat, as improvements to propellers mean more
distance traveled without using a lot of energy. This relates to the geometric and effective pitch
of the propeller. A propeller’s pitch is the distance that a propeller moves in one rotation. A
larger effective pitch means less slip, or the distance not gained by the propeller in one rotation.
Fewer slips result in fewer rotations of the propeller to go a certain distance and thus, less power
and energy used by the motor. Another facet of the propeller is the blade area ratio (BAR). The
BAR of a propeller relates the diameter of the propeller to the area of the blades. This dictates
how effective the propeller is in pushing a vessel in a medium. A larger BAR means more blade
area, meaning more thrust from the propeller, but also a lower final velocity as the propeller
introduces more drag. Having a good BAR for a propeller maximizes the thrust produced and the
velocity of the vessel.
Brushless Motor
For a variable thrust at the back of the boat, the use of brushless motors was required over
brushed motors. This is due to the intrinsic difference of the two motor types, with brushless
motors having three wires that represent the flow of electricity to and from the motor and a third
wire that acts as a signal for the ESCs to control the motor's rotational speed. Other advantages
to the use of brushless motors are their generally higher efficiency, improved torque, and
rotational speed outputs when compared to a brushed motor, where, at lower speeds, you would
only have the advantage of improved torque. The motors that were selected for use in the boat
are rated for 700Kv, meaning that for each volt that the batteries are able to contribute, the boat

Design
This year’s hull is the same as last year's, with some added improvements to the structural
integrity, and an upgraded hatch design for the lid. Multiple improvements have been made to
the electrical propulsion system, particularly in the acquisition of new motors and refined
mechanical drive system. Every design step was approached carefully using knowledge from the
many lessons learned during last year’s competition year
Lid Design
While the majority of the hull design is unchanged, the location of the propellers, drive
shaft, and gear system were changed for better retention of energy and efficiency. A new lid
design was also drafted and implemented (Figure 1). A hatch design was chosen to allow easy
access to vital components without the need to remove the entire lid. Additionally, two holes
were cut for the kill switches so that power can be shut off quickly in an emergency.

Propeller Design
Through initial research, many inefficiencies were found with last year’s propeller.
Significant slip was experienced with the tri-blade cleaver propeller. From the geometric pitch of
the blade at 4.64 inches, the slip experienced was 0.87 inches, for an effective pitch of 3.76
inches. Other coefficients were calculated, such as the blade-area-ratio (BAR), at 0.23. With
ideal values of slip being near 0 inches and a BAR being in the 0.45 to 0.65 range, multiple types
of cleaver props were looked into. However, there were no props that satisfied the criteria that
were desired. This led to more research into how to design a tri-blade propeller from scratch.
The new propeller was made using Open Prop v3.3.4, a free software program coded in
MATLAB m-files. Open Prop generates a prop (Figure 2) as well as related values seen in Table
2. Open prop does this by using given coefficients which were gathered from last year's boat
such as the drag coefficient, and theoretical values we wanted to achieve such as top speed and
motor RPMs, and attempts to solve for those values and output propeller geometry. By looking at
the values it can be determined how efficient and optimal the propeller will be. Then the
propeller geometry can be exported as slices of cross sections and exported to Solid Works as
seen in (Figure 3), these cross sections were then lofted to make the CAD model of the propeller
(Figure 4).
Having an EFFY or efficiency value as close to 0.8 was the aim of the iterative design
process. When letting Open Prop dictate the geometry based off of the most efficient values, it
created a propeller so thin the 3D printer was unable to complete the print. It was necessary to
increase the thickness just enough even if it meant decreasing the efficiency value. After multiple
propeller attempts, the final propeller in Figure 5 had a much lower EFFY (Table 2), but its
BAR and pitch was higher. When comparing this new propeller to last year's (Table 1) it can be
seen that the Pitch and BAR increased but the BAR only increased a small amount. It is expected
that the new propeller can perform better than the old one even with the lower EFFY than the
initial propeller design from open prop. This propeller can be further improved by attempting to
raise the EFFY while maintaining structural stability, which should improve the other values
mentioned as well.

Electrical and Propulsion Design
Multiple issues were found during the testing of last year’s boat including melted wires,
burnt out motors, and insufficient motor torque. All design decisions concerning part acquisition
were completed with the previous year’s lessons in mind.
Components:
● FrSky Taranis X9D Plus Transmitter
● FrSky X8R Receiver
● 2 Seal 300A OPTO ESCs
● 2 SSS 56123 V2 Brushless Motors, 700Kv, 9500W Continuous
● 2 Water Pumps
● 2 4.8V Batteries
● 4 Turnigy 6S 22.2V Li-Po Batteries
● 2 Blue Sea Systems 300A 32V Dual Circuit Switches
Maximising the power output of the motors was the main design goal of the electronic
propulsion system. This resulted in the purchase of new motors which had a lower kV of 700
compared to last year's motors which had 1250kV. A lower kV value allows for improved torque
from the motors, which was a major issue of the design last year. The overall power output of the
new motors is 9500W compared to the previous motors 4200W, almost half of the output of the
new motors. Last year’s motors burnt out due to their cheap quality and excessive current draw
caused by limited motor torque. The burnt out motors prevented the team from completing the
race last year, and led to the purchase of the new motors being a top priority for the electrical
design of the current boat.
Using the new power from our new motors, the estimated velocity of the boat is 30 mph
(Table 3). This value was found by assuming the same drag coefficient used last year of 0.012.
The found velocity value does not account for mechanical friction within the driveshaft, or
increased drag due to waves, wind, and other environmental factors.

The overall connection between the electronics is very similar to last year with two
batteries in series per motor, which connects to the kill switches and then fuses. After the fuses,
the wire is then fed to the ESCs where it connects to both the receiver and motors (Figure 6). All
16 gauge wire was swapped for 8 gauge to prevent previous wire heating problems that were
encountered last year. 4 new batteries were purchased this year to replace the 8 year old ones that
were beginning to get puffy on the edges. These new batteries were the same brand and
specifications as the old ones being 6 celled lipo batteries with 20000mAh. Each motor has two
batteries wired in series to give a maximum voltage of 50.4V, and a max current draw of 188
amps. At 50% throttle it is estimated that the batteries will last around 13 minutes, which should
give ample time to complete the course if the velocity is correct (Table 4). During the race, the
boat will not be run at full throttle in order to prolong the life of the boat, and prevent any heat
buildup issues that may occur.

Building and Fabrication
Hull Fabrication
While the main shape of the hull remains the same, cosmetic and structural improvements
were made. Old paint and epoxy were sanded away, and after the old drive system was removed,
the holes were filled with Bondo, sealant, and fiberglass. Then, a new layer of fiberglass and
epoxy was added to fill a leak at the bow, and an extra layer of structural stability. New holes
were drilled to accommodate the new drive system. Figure 8 displays the newly installed
stingers with the attached propellers.

Figure 7: Marking New Shaft Hole Locations

Figure 8: Stingers on New Drive System

Lid Fabrication
A new and improved lid was fabricated for this year’s competition, due to critiques of last
year’s design. The old design was clunky and had too many screws to unscrew in order to lift the
lid off the boat. The team spent time modeling multiple lid designs before landing on the one
chosen for this year’s competition. The lid consists of two parts: a main base that permanently
attaches to the boat with bolts, and an upper hatch that is able to hinge to allow quick and easy
access to vital components.
Similar to last year, the base of the lid was chosen to be made from ¼ inch plywood. It
was first laid down with the boat on top to trace the general shape. After cutting the stencil of the
boat, further measurements were made to trace the opening. Wood glue was mixed with sawdust
to create a sandable adhesive filler (Figure 10). This composite allowed for easy adjustability
during construction while still holding the pieces together. Once the shapes were in place, the
edges of the hatch were sanded down to create an aesthetically pleasing shape (Figure 12).
Figures 13 and 14 illustrate how the lid opens and closes to facilitate quick access to
components.

Figure 9. Hatch opening being cut

being applied to the inside of hatch

Propeller Fabrication
Propellers were 3D printed in halves, aligned using a small amount of epoxy, then
covered in epoxy before being sanded and balanced. Multiple props were fabricated in an
iterative design process. Sacrificial parts were modeled onto the props so they could be used as a
stand during the sealing process, and broken off afterward.

Figure 19: 3D Printed Propellers
Testing
Multiple tests of the boat and its systems have been performed. Motors and wires operate
significantly cooler than last year’s boat due to the new water scoop intakes, higher quality
motors, and higher gauge wires. Thrust and speed performance are at least twice as much as last
year’s boat. New propellers are still in the testing phase, and are not reliable enough to use in full
scale lake testing. Epoxy is brittle and any propellor imbalance will rip the propellor apart.
Different materials such as carbon fiber and fiberglass threads will be experimented with in the
future to create the optimal composite propeller. For now, the old machined 3 bladed, 2.9 inch
propellers will be used.

pages.text:
Risk
Managing risk was an important topic during the design process. Multiple design
decisions were executed to mitigate the amount of risk during operation and fabrication. Kill
switches are now accessible from the outside of the boat (Figure 22), which will lead to a safer
environment during testing and use. Two fuses are installed on each motor drive system right
after the batteries to prevent damaging components and excessive heat buildup. All 12 gauge
wire was replaced with 8 gauge which can handle a higher heat, improving safety and reducing
risk. Empty compartments of the boat towards the bow are filled with foam to provide buoyancy
if the hull fails, batteries are secured to the boat with velcro (Figure 23), and a tow hook is
installed at the bow (Figure 24). This will allow for safe recovery of the boat in the event of
sinkage or hull damage, and prevent toxic components such as batteries to be stuck at the bottom
of the lake. During operation of the boat, great care is taken to ensure all members are safely
away from the props. A safety switch on the transmitter will cut all throttle to the motors if
necessary, and a kill signal will be sent if signal is lost.

Risk
        Managing risk was an important topic during the design process. Multiple design
decisions were executed to mitigate the amount of risk during operation and fabrication. Kill
switches are now accessible from the outside of the boat (Figure 22), which will lead to a safer
environment during testing and use. Two fuses are installed on each motor drive system right
after the batteries to prevent damaging components and excessive heat buildup. All 12 gauge
wire was replaced with 8 gauge which can handle a higher heat, improving safety and reducing
risk. Empty compartments of the boat towards the bow are filled with foam to provide buoyancy
if the hull fails, batteries are secured to the boat with velcro (Figure 23), and a tow hook is
installed at the bow (Figure 24). This will allow for safe recovery of the boat in the event of
sinkage or hull damage, and prevent toxic components such as batteries to be stuck at the bottom
of the lake. During operation of the boat, great care is taken to ensure all members are safely
away from the props. A safety switch on the transmitter will cut all throttle to the motors if
necessary, and a kill signal will be sent if signal is lost.
